```{r, include = FALSE}
# Figures are drawn on the real CPB canvas (half page is 7.5 cm, full
# page is 15.5 cm) and only displayed smaller. Code is hidden by default
# so that readers who do not use R see the figure and its parameters.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7.5 / 2.54,
  fig.height = 7.5 / 2.54,
  dpi = 300,
  out.width = "100%",
  dev = if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) "ragg_png" else "png",
  dev.args = list(background = "#eef8ff")
)

# LATER WILL USE THIS WORKFLOW IN THE MARKDOWN WHEN THE M-PATH IS KNOWN:
# 1. Find the most recent ggcpb folder in `[path]`.
# 2. Copy it to the place where you want to create figures.
# 3. Put your datasets in the folder `data`. Open `params.csv` in Excel
#    and describe your figures.
# 4. Start `generate_plot.bat` by
#    double clicking it. Your figures appear in the folder `generated`.

```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(conflicted)
library(ggcpb)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
set.seed(42)

# Shows the parameters that build a figure, as a small table.
ptab <- function(...) {
  p <- list(...)
  knitr::kable(data.frame(parameter = names(p), value = unlist(p),
                          row.names = NULL),
               align = "l", format = "html", col.names = NULL,
               table.attr = 'class="ptab"')
}

# One standard sentence under every figure. `section` is the number of the
# example code at the end, which the sentence links to (`id` is its anchor).
repro <- function(fun, dataset, section, id) {
  cat("<span class=\"repro-title\">**How to reproduce this figure:**</span> ",
      "copy `params.csv`, `generate_plot.bat` ",
      "and the folder `data` with `", dataset, ".csv` to a personal folder. ",
      "Fill in the parameters above in `params.csv` and start the script. ",
      "In R you can call `", fun, "()` instead. Follow the example code in ",
      "[section ", section, "](#", id, ") to create the plot in R. ",
      "Alternatively, the csv file can be read with `read.csv()` and used ",
      "as input to `", fun, "()`.\n", sep = "")
}
```

This vignette gives a short introduction to creating customizable
CPB style figures with ggcpb.

# What is ggcpb?

ggcpb is the new version of James. It draws figures in the 
CPB house style from Excel or from R. 


## Why ggcpb instead of James?

ggcpb is more future proof. It is built on ggplot2, the most widely
used plotting package in R. This brings the following benefits:

* **More possibilities.** Anything ggplot2 can do, ggcpb can do. If you
  need an extra layer or a special annotation, you can add it. 
  It allows for new figure types that were not possible with James,
  such as a donut chart.
* **Easier to maintain.** ggcpb adds a thin layer to a well tested
  package.

## What you need to know to use ggcpb in Excel

This is the general workflow to create figures with ggcpb without using R:

1. Find the most recent ggcpb version.
2. Copy it to the place where you want to create figures.
3. Put your datasets in the folder `data`. 
   Open `params.csv` in Excel and describe your figures.
4. Start `generate_plot.bat` by double clicking it. This runs the `generate_plot.R` script.
   Your figures appear in the folder `generated`. Each image is named after
   its dataset. Running the script again produces updated figures. 
   Images with the same name are replaced. A dataset or figure that 
   fails is skipped and listed at the end, and in `params_log.txt`. 
   The other figures are still saved.

*Please note*. The `generate_plot.bat`, `generate_plot.R` and `params.csv` must all be 
in the same folder. Within this folder, there must be a subfolder `data`,
in which each dataset must be saved as a CSV file, and *not* as spreadsheet (`xlsx`).
In Excel, choose `File` -> `Save as` -> `CSV UTF-8 (comma delimited)`.

You do not need to know R to follow this workflow. One parameter file and
one or more datasets drive everything.

* `params.csv` describes your figures. Column 1 holds the parameter
  names, such as `title`, `x` and `data`. Every other column describes
  one figure. The row `data` names the dataset of the figure. All parameters 
  and their descriptions are given in the [import vignette](import.md).
* The folder `data` holds your datasets. Each dataset is its own CSV
  file with any name, such as `koopkracht.csv`. The first row holds the
  column names. The following rows are the observations per column.

Add the row `page` to save a figure at `full` width (15.5 cm). The
default is `half` (7.5 cm). Write the dataset name without `.csv`, such as `koopkracht`. Leave
`data` blank to use `data/data.csv`. Write `a;b` to draw the same
figure for both datasets. A figure is saved under the name of its
dataset, so `koopkracht` gives `koopkracht.png`. If
two figures use the same dataset, the figure number is added, such as
`koopkracht_1.png`.

Run the script again after every change. This will update the figures. The
import vignette gives a more detailed explanation
and lists all settings per figure type.
See [`vignette("import")`](import.html).

## Use ggcpb in R

Next to plotting Excel data with ggcpb, you can also plot data that
you already have in R. The caption below each figure in this introduction
shows the function to use. Load the packages first.

```{r library, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
library(conflicted) # optional, but recommended
library(ggcpb)
```

Each figure type has its own function.

```{r functions, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# Line chart
cpb_line(data = df, x = year, y = value)
# Bar chart
cpb_col(data = df, x = year, y = value, fill = group)
# Area chart
cpb_area(data = df, x = year, y = value, fill = group)
# Box plot
cpb_box(data = df, x = group, p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95)
# Dot plot
cpb_dot(data = df, x = term, y = estimate, lower = lower, upper = upper)
# Donut chart
cpb_donut(data = df, fill = group, y = share)
# Scatter plot
cpb_scatter(data = df, x = income, y = spending)
# Histogram
cpb_hist(data = df, x = duration)
# Map
cpb_map(data = df, region = code, value = share)
```

To export a figure, use `save_cpb()`. It writes the figure at the CPB
page widths. Use `page = "half"` for 7.5 cm and `page = "full"` for
15.5 cm.

```{r save, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
save_cpb("zonnepanelen.png", p, page = "half")
```

The rest of this introduction assumes that you work in Excel.

# Figure types

Each figure below is combined with a feature that you can also use
with several other plot types, if not all. The parameters and their 
corresponding values are portrayed next to the figure. Other settings keep their default.

The style of the figures can be set for a whole publication. See
[section 4](#publication-settings).

## Line with forecast

A line chart with a forecast window and an uncertainty band.

```{r data-line}
groei <- tibble(jaar = 2015:2027,
                groei = round(rnorm(13, 1.5, 0.8), 1)) |>
  mutate(marge = c(rep(0, 9), 0.4, 0.9, 1.4, 1.8),
         lo = groei - marge, hi = groei + marge)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r line-forecast}
cpb_line(groei, x = jaar, y = groei, ymin = lo, ymax = hi,
         forecast_x = 2023.5,
         title = "Economische groei met onzekerheid", ylab = "%") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2027, 3), minor_breaks = 2015:2027,
                     guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE))
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-line}
ptab(plot_type = "line", title = "Economische groei met onzekerheid",
     x = "jaar", y = "groei", ymin = "lo", ymax = "hi",
     forecast_x = 2023.5, ylab = "%")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_line", "line-forecast", "5.1", "code-line-forecast")
```

## Columns with two axes

Two series on one figure, with the second series on the right axis.
The legend tells you which axis belongs to which series.

```{r data-col}
erfenissen <- expand_grid(
  soort = factor(c("geen aangifte", "wel aangifte"),
                 levels = c("geen aangifte", "wel aangifte")),
  jaar  = 2015:2022
) |>
  mutate(mld = c(15.0, 15.3, 15.5, 16.3, 19.4, 20.5, 22.2, 23.0,
                 5.8, 5.6, 5.6, 6.6, 6.4, 6.5, 6.8, 7.0)) |>
  left_join(tibble(jaar = 2015:2022,
                   heffing = c(1.7, 1.8, 1.8, 1.8, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6)),
            by = "jaar")
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r col-secaxis, warning = FALSE}
cpb_col(erfenissen, x = jaar, y = mld, fill = soort,
        sec_y = heffing, sec_limits = c(0, 3),
        sec_legend_label = "erfbelasting", sec_ylab = "mld euro",
        title = "Erfenissen en erfbelasting", ylab = "mld euro")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-col}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Erfenissen en erfbelasting",
     x = "jaar", y = "mld", fill = "soort", sec_y = "heffing",
     sec_limits = "0;3", sec_legend_label = "erfbelasting",
     sec_ylab = "mld euro", ylab = "mld euro")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "col-secaxis", "5.2", "code-col-secaxis")
```

## Horizontal bars with chosen colours

The colours decide the legend. Pick them with `colour_index`.

```{r data-hbar}
groepen <- c("tot 120% wml", "120% wml tot modaal", "1 tot 1,5x modaal",
             "1,5 tot 2x modaal", "2 tot 3x modaal", "boven 3x modaal")
zonnepanelen <- expand_grid(
  jaar  = factor(c(2021, 2024), levels = c(2024, 2021)),
  groep = factor(groepen, levels = rev(groepen))
) |>
  mutate(aandeel = c(10, 14, 19, 22, 26, 33,
                     19, 25, 31, 38, 47, 59))
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r col-horizontal}
cpb_col(zonnepanelen, x = groep, y = aandeel, fill = jaar,
        position = "dodge", orientation = "horizontal",
        colour_index = c(2, 1), value_limits = c(0, 70), width = 0.85,
        title = "Zonnepanelen naar inkomen",
        ylab  = "inkomensgroep", xlab = "aandeel binnen inkomensgroep (%)")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-hbar}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Zonnepanelen naar inkomen",
     x = "groep", y = "aandeel", fill = "jaar", position = "dodge",
     orientation = "horizontal", colour_index = "2;1",
     value_limits = "0;70", ylab = "inkomensgroep",
     xlab = "aandeel binnen inkomensgroep (%)")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "col-horizontal", "5.3", "code-col-horizontal")
```

## Line with markers in English

A line with markers suits a few ordered categories. This figure uses
the English style.

```{r data-points}
leeftijden <- c("20 to 30", "30 to 40", "40 to 50", "50 to 60", "60 to 70")
tarieven <- expand_grid(
  erfenis  = factor(c("10,000 euro", "100,000 euro"),
                    levels = c("10,000 euro", "100,000 euro")),
  leeftijd = factor(leeftijden, levels = leeftijden)
) |>
  mutate(tarief = c(14.5, 12.5, 13.5, 10.5, 8.5,
                    21.5, 18.5, 18.5, 17.5, 17.5))
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r line-points}
cpb_line(tarieven, x = leeftijd, y = tarief, colour = erfenis,
         points = TRUE, value_limits = c(0, 30), style = "english",
         title = "Preferred tax rate by age", ylab = "% average rate")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-points}
ptab(plot_type = "line", title = "Preferred tax rate by age",
     x = "leeftijd", y = "tarief", colour = "erfenis", points = "TRUE",
     value_limits = "0;30", style = "english", ylab = "% average rate")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_line", "line-points", "5.4", "code-line-points")
```

## Boxplot

A box shows the 25th to 75th percentile. The line in the box is the
median. The whiskers run from the 5th to the 95th percentile.

```{r data-box}
raw <- tibble(
  groep      = factor(rep(groepen, each = 400), levels = rev(groepen)),
  koopkracht = rnorm(2400, mean = rep(c(-3, -1.5, 0, 1, 2, 3.5), each = 400),
                     sd = 2)
)
kk <- raw |>
  summarise(p5 = quantile(koopkracht, 0.05), p25 = quantile(koopkracht, 0.25),
            p50 = quantile(koopkracht, 0.50), p75 = quantile(koopkracht, 0.75),
            p95 = quantile(koopkracht, 0.95), .by = groep)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r box}
cpb_box(kk, x = groep,
        p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
        orientation = "horizontal",
        title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep",
        subtitle = "inkomensgroep", ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-box}
ptab(plot_type = "box", title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep",
     x = "groep", p5 = "p5", p25 = "p25", p50 = "p50", p75 = "p75",
     p95 = "p95", orientation = "horizontal",
     subtitle = "inkomensgroep", ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_box", "box", "5.5", "code-box")
```

More box plot styles are in [`vignette("boxplots")`](boxplots.html).

## Extended boxplot on a full page

The extended boxplot has the CPB ramingen-style. Through the `facet` parameter the data gets grouped into the year column,
which results in one panel per year in the dataset.
The default figure is saved at the full
page width (15.5 cm) with `page = full`.

```{r data-box-extended}
kk_jaar <- bind_rows(
  mutate(kk, jaar = "2024"),
  mutate(kk, jaar = "2025", across(p5:p95, \(v) v + 0.5))
)
```

```{r box-extended, fig.width = 15.5 / 2.54, fig.height = 7.5 / 2.54}
cpb_boxplot_extended(kk_jaar, x = groep,
                     p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
                     facet = jaar, facet_ncol = 2,
                     title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep",
                     ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

::: {.below}

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-box-extended}
ptab(plot_type = "boxplot_extended", title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep",
     x = "groep", p5 = "p5", p25 = "p25", p50 = "p50", p75 = "p75",
     p95 = "p95", facet = "jaar", facet_ncol = 2,
     ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie", page = "full")
```

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_boxplot_extended", "box-extended", "5.6", "code-box-extended")
```

## Donut chart

Individual categories add up to 100% in the donut chart. 
Categories don't need to be expressed as percentages.
Any numerical values will work, as the donut chart 
automatically calculates the proportions.

```{r data-donut}
bronnen <- c("gas", "elektriciteit", "warmte", "overig")
energie <- tibble(bron = factor(bronnen, levels = bronnen),
                  aandeel = c(45, 30, 15, 10))
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r donut, warning = FALSE}
cpb_donut(energie, fill = bron, y = aandeel,
          colour_index = c(6, 5, 2, 4),
          title = "Energiemix van huishoudens")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-donut}
ptab(plot_type = "donut", title = "Energiemix van huishoudens",
     fill = "bron", y = "aandeel", colour_index = "6;5;2;4")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_donut", "donut", "5.7", "code-donut")
```

## Dot plot

A dot plot shows an estimate with its interval.

With `legend = filled-empty` the figure has no legend, but it keeps the
space of one. This gives the same panel height as a figure with a legend.

```{r data-dot}
termen <- c("Werken ontmoedigd", "Ongelijkheid", "Hard werken loont",
            "Leeftijd", "Geslacht", "Kinderen")
schatting <- tibble(
  term = factor(termen, levels = termen),
  blok = factor(rep(c("Percepties", "Achtergrond"), each = 3),
                levels = c("Percepties", "Achtergrond")),
  coef = c(3.2, 2.9, -2.0, 3.5, 0.4, -1.4),
  lo   = c(-0.3, 2.1, -3.0, 2.6, -1.3, -3.3),
  hi   = c(6.6, 3.6, -1.1, 4.3, 2.2, 0.6)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r dot}
cpb_dot(schatting, x = term, y = coef, lower = lo, upper = hi,
        group = blok, legend = "filled-empty",
        title = "Samenhang met voorkeurstarieven",
        xlab  = "%punt verandering")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-dot}
ptab(plot_type = "dot", title = "Samenhang met voorkeurstarieven",
     x = "term", y = "coef", lower = "lo", upper = "hi", group = "blok",
     legend = "filled-empty", xlab = "%punt verandering")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_dot", "dot", "5.8", "code-dot")
```

## Scatter plot

The parameter `cut` puts the purchasing power change into classes. The
classes give the points their colour.

```{r data-scatter}
hh <- tibble(inkomen = round(rlnorm(400, log(2500), 0.35))) |>
  mutate(energierekening = round(90 + 0.04 * inkomen + rnorm(n(), 0, 35)),
         koopkracht      = round(rnorm(n(), (inkomen - 2500) / 1500, 2), 1))
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r scatter}
cpb_scatter(hh, x = inkomen, y = energierekening,
            colour = cpb_cut(koopkracht, c(-Inf, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, Inf),
                             labeller = label_pct_nl()),
            palette = "discr",
            legend_ncol = 2,
            title = "Energierekening naar inkomen",
            ylab  = "energierekening (euro per maand)",
            xlab  = "besteedbaar inkomen (euro per maand)",
            x_labels = label_euro_nl(),
            legend_title = "koopkracht (%)")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-scatter}
ptab(plot_type = "scatter", title = "Energierekening naar inkomen",
     x = "inkomen", y = "energierekening", colour = "koopkracht",
     cut = "-Inf;-2;-1;0;1;2;Inf", cut_labels = "pct", palette = "discr",
     legend_ncol = 2, ylab = "energierekening (euro per maand)",
     xlab = "besteedbaar inkomen (euro per maand)", x_labels = "euro",
     legend_title = "koopkracht (%)")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_scatter", "scatter", "5.9", "code-scatter")
```

## Classed map

The maps can display municipalities or provinces 
on bundled generalised CBS/Kadaster boundaries.
The following map colours each Dutch municipality by class. 
The parameter `cut` makes the classes,
and `cut_labels = pct` writes them as percentages.
In R, `cpb_cut()` and `label_pct_nl()` do the same.
The boundaries come with the package.

```{r data-map, echo = TRUE}
gemeenten <- tibble(code = unique(cpb_nl_geo("gemeente")$code)) |>
  mutate(aandeel = runif(n(), 5, 75),
         klasse  = cpb_cut(aandeel, breaks = c(0, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, Inf),
                           labeller = label_pct_nl()))
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r map, warning = FALSE}
cpb_map(gemeenten, region = code, value = klasse,
        palette = "blues",
        title = "Aandeel huishoudens met zonnepanelen",
        legend_title = "aandeel")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-map}
ptab(plot_type = "map", title = "Aandeel huishoudens met zonnepanelen",
     region = "code", value = "aandeel", cut = "0;20;30;40;50;60;Inf",
     cut_labels = "pct", palette = "blues", legend_title = "aandeel")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_map", "map", "5.11", "code-map")
```

More options are in [`vignette("maps")`](maps.html).

# Ggplot2 base allows for endless possibilities

Every ggcpb figure is a real ggplot2 object. This means you can stack
extra functionalities to the plot in R with `+`.

The next figure has a sharp rise between 2020 and 2021. We add a
reference line, and a text along the diagonal in dark pink italic
letters. The position comes from the coordinates of the data. The
`angle` follows the slope of the line.

```{r diagonal, echo = TRUE, out.width = "50%"}
stijging <- tibble(jaar = 2017:2024,
                   waarde = c(2.1, 2.3, 2.0, 1.9, 6.4, 6.8, 6.5, 6.6))

cpb_line(stijging, x = jaar, y = waarde,
         title = "Een scherpe stijging", ylab = "%") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2020.2, y = 4.2, label = "scherpe stijging",
           angle = 72, colour = "#a0004e", fontface = "italic",
           size = 2.4, family = cpb_font_family())
```


You can stack as many pieces as you need. More patterns are in
[`vignette("annotation")`](annotation.html).

<a id="publication-settings"></a>

# Settings for the whole publication

Some settings are the same for every figure of a publication. The main one
is the `style`. Dutch is the default. An English report uses `english`.
It sets the number format and the words, such as the forecast label.

In R, set it once at the start of the script. Every figure then uses it,
unless a figure sets its own `style`.

```{r publication-style, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
options(ggcpb.style = "dutch") # or "english"
```

In Excel there is no single setting for all figures. Add the row `style` to
`params.csv` and give every figure the same value in its column, such as
`english`. A blank cell uses the Dutch default.

# Example code to create figures in R

The code below creates the figures above in R. It first builds the data,
then draws the figure. It is the same code that made the figures in this
document. Start the script with these lines.

```{r code-library, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
library(conflicted)
library(ggcpb)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

options(ggcpb.style = "dutch") # style of the whole publication
```
